details.label: Discussion
details.text: Early afternoon visible satellite shows a growing cumulus field and isolated thunderstorm development from south-central MO through northwest AR into northeast OK along a weak surface front in the area. Ahead of the front, temperatures have warmed into the mid to upper 90s, which, combined with boundary-layer dewpoints in the upper 60s to mid 70s, is yielding MLCAPE of 2000-3000 J/kg with a weakening cap. In the absence of appreciable forcing for ascent, continued heating and convergence along the front are expected to foster a gradual increase in storms and related severe weather risk over the next 1-2 hours amidst a weakly sheared environment (i.e., bulk shear magnitudes of generally less than 30 kt), per regional VWPs. As such, the severe threat should remain somewhat isolated at least initially with the primary hazards being locally damaging winds with gusts of 60-65 mph and marginally severe hail. Time-lagged HRRR and RRFS ensemble guidance has shown a consistent signal for storm clustering to occur by late afternoon into early evening, at which point the damaging wind threat could increase in areal extent. A separate area of severe storms may materialize later this afternoon over the ArkLaTex, ahead of a surface low and multiple MCVs approaching the region from the west/northwest. Here, too the environment is expected to become supportive of some wind and hail risk

details.label: Discussion
details.text: Latest surface analysis places an occluded low across southern Ontario with a cold front extending south-southwestward across Lake Michigan and into central Illinois as of 1700 UTC. Dewpoints generally range from the low to mid-60s F ahead of this front, with modest moisture pooling and greater dewpoints (low 70s F) noted in the immediate vicinity of the boundary across central IL. As this front progresses eastward through the afternoon, ongoing surface heating and southeasterly low-level theta-e advection will yield an eastward transition of a relatively narrow and destabilizing corridor of 1000 to locally 2000 J/kg MLCAPE. Expectation is for some intensification to occur with ongoing convection across southwestern Michigan over the next 1-2 hours, with additional initiation likely farther southwest along the cold front (where deepening cumulus are currently noted on visible satellite imagery). Effective shear of 25-30 kts is sufficient to support multicellular clusters and perhaps marginal supercell structures capable of primarily damaging wind gusts (generally 50-60 mph) and large hail. A brief tornado cannot be ruled out, but veered low-level winds should largely temper this risk. The need for a watch remains somewhat unclear owing to generally limited effective shear and thus uncertainty regarding overall convective intensity

details.label: Discussion
details.text: A sub-severe MCS is ongoing across portions of western and middle TN as of late morning with a southeastward motion of 25-30 kt. Visible satellite imagery indicates additional deepening cumulus and incipient thunderstorm development over portions of eastern MS and western AL, in the vicinity of a weak quasi-stationary boundary analyzed in that area. The air mass across the discussion area is characterized by temperatures in the mid 80s to lower 90s with dewpoints in the upper 60s to mid 70s, yielding MLCAPE up to 1500-2500 J/kg, per latest objective analysis. Latest model guidance indicates a gradual increase in storm coverage this afternoon along the cold pool/gust front associated with the MCS as well as in the vicinity of the stationary front mentioned above. Weak mid-level lapse rates and vertical shear are expected to limit the potential for an organized severe weather threat. However, steepening low-level lapse rates and the presence of a relatively moist environment (PW of 1.8-2 inches) suggest the potential for locally intense wet microbursts capable of damaging wind gusts
